inputs.need:
I am a general surgeon at a regional hospital where we perform about 620 elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies a year, and we want most of these patients to go home the same day. At present 58 percent of patients booked as day cases go home the same evening; the rest stay overnight, most often for nausea and vomiting, pain, a late finish on the list, or a drain. Our day surgery unit wants a short list of predictors it can use at booking to decide who should be placed early on the list or planned for an overnight stay from the start, instead of converting patients at six in the evening.

My plan was a retrospective chart review of all elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies from 2019 to 2025 using the electronic health record and the theatre management system. Our anaesthesia chief argues that the charts are unreliable for what matters most, such as how bad the nausea was and when the patient first walked, and that we should collect data prospectively for a year with a standard discharge-readiness assessment. I need help deciding between the two, choosing candidate predictors without overfitting, handling list order and surgeon effects, and making sure the result is something the booking nurses can use. We have no research funding beyond an analyst from the hospital's decision support team, and the day surgery unit wants recommendations for its 2028 scheduling cycle.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; one decision support analyst for about 20 days; recommendations are needed for the day surgery unit's 2028 scheduling cycle; any prospective data collection would need nursing time that is not yet funded.

records.title: Predictors of failed same-day discharge after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a retrospective analysis of 2,940 procedures
records.authors: Achterberg-Kamau P, Lindqvist-Ferreira J, Osei-Whitlock D
records.abstract: We reviewed 2,940 elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies booked as day cases at two hospitals. Same-day discharge failed in 21 percent. Age over 70, higher anaesthetic risk class, a start after 13:00, nausea needing rescue treatment and placement of a drain were associated with failure. A model with nine predictors had a c statistic of 0.72 in the development data. The model was not validated in other data, the authors selected predictors partly by statistical significance, and several candidate variables had more than 20 percent missing values.

records.title: Operating list position and same-day discharge after day-case cholecystectomy
records.abstract: In 1,810 day-case cholecystectomies, same-day discharge failed in 38 percent of operations starting after 14:00 and in 14 percent of those starting before 11:00. After adjustment for patient factors, a start after 14:00 remained strongly associated with overnight stay. Patients placed late on the list were older and had more comorbidities in one of the two hospitals, suggesting that list order was partly chosen by risk. The authors recommend that booking rules consider both patient risk and list position rather than treating list position as fixed.

records.title: Chart documentation of postoperative nausea and mobilisation after day surgery: agreement with direct observation
records.abstract: Trained observers recorded nausea severity and the time of first mobilisation for 420 day surgery patients and compared them with the clinical record. Nausea severity was documented in 41 percent of charts, and the time of first mobilisation in 36 percent. When documented, nausea severity agreed moderately with observation. Administration of a rescue antiemetic was recorded for almost every patient who received one. The authors conclude that charts are a poor source for nausea severity and mobilisation times but that medication records may serve as a proxy.

records.title: Rescue antiemetic administration as a proxy for postoperative nausea and vomiting in electronic records: a validation study
records.abstract: We compared rescue antiemetic doses recorded in the electronic medication record with nurse-assessed postoperative nausea and vomiting in 1,120 day surgery patients. Agreement for clinically important nausea or vomiting was good (kappa 0.71). The proxy missed patients whose nausea was managed without medication and counted some doses given for prevention after a first episode. Agreement was similar across surgical specialties. The authors suggest the proxy is suitable for research on nausea severe enough to need treatment, but not for mild nausea.

records.title: Surgeon variation in same-day discharge after laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multilevel analysis
records.abstract: Across 4,380 day-case cholecystectomies by 31 surgeons, the intraclass correlation for same-day discharge failure at the surgeon level was 0.09 after adjustment for patient factors and list position. Surgeon-level variation was explained partly by drain use and by the timing of the first postoperative review. Surgeons with lower failure rates more often discharged patients directly from the recovery area. The authors recommend accounting for surgeon clustering in prediction and quality work and caution against ranking surgeons on unadjusted rates or small numbers of cases.

records.title: Prediction models for discharge after day-case surgery: a systematic review of development and validation
records.authors: Mistry-Okonkwo A, Castellanos-Brandt E, Nwosu-Lindgren F
records.abstract: We identified 14 prediction models for failed discharge after day-case surgery. Eleven were at high risk of bias, most often because of too few events for the number of candidate predictors (median 6 events per candidate predictor), selection of predictors by significance and no correction for optimism. Only three models were validated in data from another period or hospital, and their c statistics fell by 0.05 to 0.11. Calibration was reported for four models. The authors recommend pre-specified predictors, penalised estimation and temporal or external validation.

records.title: A nurse-led discharge readiness assessment after day surgery: a prospective cohort
records.abstract: In 760 day surgery patients, nurses completed a standard discharge readiness assessment four hours after surgery, covering nausea, pain, mobilisation, voiding and escort. Of patients assessed as ready, 88 percent went home the same day. The assessment took a median of 6 minutes. Patients assessed as not ready most often had nausea or had not yet walked. The assessment required a nurse dedicated to recovery follow-up for the study period, which the unit could not sustain afterwards, and assessments were missed on days when that nurse was absent.

records.title: Patients' views on same-day discharge after gallbladder surgery
records.abstract: We spoke with 24 patients who had day-case gallbladder surgery, of whom 9 stayed overnight unexpectedly. Patients wanted to know in advance whether an overnight stay was likely so they could arrange transport and care at home. Those converted to an overnight stay late in the evening described frustration and poor sleep on a busy ward. Patients living alone or far from the hospital were most worried about going home the same day. Participants came from one hospital and volunteered after a postal invitation.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Booking-time predictors of failed same-day discharge are plausible (age, anaesthetic risk, rescue-treated nausea, drains, list position), but most published prediction models are at high risk of bias from too few events per candidate predictor and lack validation. Charts document nausea severity and mobilisation poorly, which supports the case for prospective data, yet rescue antiemetic doses in medication records are a validated proxy for nausea needing treatment. List position is strongly associated with failure and is partly chosen by risk, and surgeons cluster. A nurse-led readiness assessment gives good data but needs dedicated nursing time. Patients want advance warning of an overnight stay.
response.gradeRationale: Observational development studies at risk of bias, one review of models, and validation evidence for one proxy; certainty about which predictors will perform locally is low.

The retrieved evidence says charts miss nausea severity and mobilisation, but that rescue antiemetic doses are a validated proxy, and that most published models fail through too few events and no validation.

response.designSummary: Prediction model development from a 12-month prospective cohort.
response.sampleSize: About 620 procedures in 12 months with about 42 percent overnight stays give about 260 events. The surgeons' candidate list has 18 parameters once surgeon, list position categories and splines for age are counted, giving about 14 events per candidate parameter. That is enough to fit a penalised model but leaves no independent data for validation: a split would halve the events, and a temporal validation would need a second year of prospective collection, beyond the 2028 scheduling cycle. The retrieved review found that models validated on later data lost 0.05 to 0.11 in c statistic, so an unvalidated model would overstate performance.

response.overview: Retrospective development of a booking-time prediction model for failed same-day discharge after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, using 2019 to 2023 records for development and 2024 to 2025 records for temporal validation.
response.population: All adults booked for elective day-case laparoscopic cholecystectomy from January 2019 to December 2025 (about 3,690 procedures); first procedure per patient.
response.exposure: Pre-specified booking-time predictors: age, anaesthetic risk class, body mass index, previous nausea with anaesthesia, diabetes, living alone, travel distance and planned list position (first half or second half, and start after 13:00).

Nausea needing treatment is taken from rescue antiemetic doses in the medication record, checked first against 100 randomly sampled charts. Time of first walking, available from mid-2021, is used only in a sensitivity analysis. Surgeon is recorded for clustering.

response.designSummary: Development of a penalised logistic model on 2019 to 2023 records and temporal validation on 2024 to 2025 records, with surgeon clustering.
response.sampleSize: Development data from 2019 to 2023 hold about 2,600 procedures and, at about 42 percent failure, about 1,100 events; with eight pre-specified predictors and about 12 parameters after categories and splines, that is about 90 events per parameter, well above the level at which the retrieved review found overfitting (median 6 events per candidate predictor). Minimum sample size criteria for a model of this size (expected shrinkage of at least 0.9 and precise estimation of the overall risk) are met with a wide margin. The 2024 to 2025 validation set holds about 1,050 procedures and about 440 events, above the usual minimum of 200 events for precise calibration.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic regression with ridge penalisation on the pre-specified predictors, age modelled with restricted cubic splines, surgeon as a random intercept in a sensitivity model, and bootstrap optimism correction for apparent performance.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Temporal validation: c statistic, calibration intercept and slope, and a calibration plot on 2024 to 2025; decision curve analysis for booking thresholds; sensitivity analysis adding time of first walking from mid-2021; calibration reported for patients living alone and for those living more than an hour away.
response.missingData: Body mass index and living alone are expected to be missing in about 8 percent; multiple imputation by chained equations with 20 imputations including the outcome, with imputation applied separately in development and validation data.
response.multiplicity: Not applicable to a prediction model; no significance testing of individual predictors.
response.software: R with rms, glmnet and mice.
overfittingGuards: Penalised estimation with bootstrap optimism correction

response.summary: About 1,100 development events and 440 validation events support a penalised model with temporal validation.

response.risks: Low: secondary use of existing records. A booking model could disadvantage patients if it steers older or isolated patients away from day surgery without reason.
response.consent: Individual consent is impracticable for about 3,690 past procedures; the work proceeds under data access approval DAC-2026-51 with a request to the research ethics board for a waiver of consent.
response.data: Extraction on the hospital analytics server; record numbers replaced by study codes; no data leave the hospital.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, patients living alone and those living far from the hospital are more likely to be predicted to stay. Calibration is reported for these groups, and the booking rule offers planning support (transport, early list position) rather than excluding them from day surgery.
response.effectiveness: Success is a validated, calibrated booking tool the unit can use in its 2028 scheduling cycle.
response.efficiency: About 20 analyst days and existing data.
response.grants: None needed; an evaluation of booking changes informed by the model could seek hospital improvement funding.
response.partnerships: Booking nurses, surgeons, the anaesthesia chief, the day surgery unit manager and a patient partner who stayed overnight unexpectedly.
response.rebPath: Research ethics board review with a request for waiver of consent for secondary use, under the TCPS 2 and ICH-GCP principles; the data access approval is in place.
response.limitations: Proxy measure of nausea; practice drift over seven years; list position partly chosen by risk.

response.title: Booking-time prediction of failed same-day discharge after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy: development and temporal validation
response.abstract: Objective: to develop and temporally validate a booking-time model predicting failed same-day discharge after elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Design: retrospective development on 2019 to 2023 records and validation on 2024 to 2025 records at one hospital. Predictors: eight pre-specified booking-time variables including planned list position. Results and conclusions will be written after the analysis.
response.introduction: Many patients booked as day cases stay overnight after late conversion. Published models are mostly at high risk of bias and rarely validated, and charts record nausea poorly, although medication records offer a validated proxy.
response.methods: Penalised logistic regression with pre-specified predictors, bootstrap optimism correction, surgeon clustering in a sensitivity model, and temporal validation with calibration and decision curves. Nausea needing treatment is measured from rescue antiemetic doses, checked against sampled charts. TRIPOD reporting.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present the cohort flow, model coefficients, apparent and optimism-corrected performance, validation discrimination and calibration, and decision curves.
response.discussion: The discussion will consider how the unit could use the model at booking, the limits of the nausea proxy, practice drift and the non-causal meaning of list position.
response.limitations: One hospital; proxy measurement of nausea; list position partly chosen by risk.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not claim that moving patients on the list reduces overnight stays.
